answer.summary: Five similar past cases were found, all classified as TRANSPORT_QOS, and all show elevated jitter, latency and packet loss with call drops in the degraded range. Two of them also show MOBILITY_HANDOVER and three show CONGESTION_CAPACITY, so backhaul congestion is the most consistent pattern in the data. The priority is estimated as P4 (Low) from median KPIs because no KPI values were supplied, and the case correlations do not establish causation.

recommendations.action: Check interface counters on the site router and aggregation devices for errors, discards and CRC failures. For microwave links, check received signal level and modulation; for fibre, check optical power.
recommendations.rationale: Separates a physical or interface fault from a capacity problem.

recommendations.action: Review recent transport changes, including routing, QoS policies and maintenance windows, for anything that coincides with the onset of symptoms.
recommendations.rationale: A routing or QoS change can produce this exact symptom set without any capacity or hardware fault.

recommendations.rationale: Targets the jitter and call quality symptoms directly; the runbook lists it as an immediate action.

recommendations.action: If a backup or protection path is available, reroute traffic to it. This changes the network and requires change approval.
recommendations.rationale: Immediate relief if the primary path is congested or degraded.

recommendations.action: Repair or replace degraded physical components, correct any duplex or MTU mismatches, and increase backhaul capacity if utilization is the confirmed cause. Then set alerts on latency, jitter and loss trends.
recommendations.rationale: Addresses the root cause and prevents recurrence, following the short-term and preventive runbook actions.

- Monitor transport KPIs continuously with alerts on latency, jitter and loss trends.

supporting_evidence: Performance model: observed throughput 410.337 Mbps vs expected 682.3 Mbps (deficit -39.9%, below_expected)
Similar cases CASE-000876 and CASE-031577 are TRANSPORT_QOS+CONGESTION_CAPACITY, both showing packet loss at crit level
Segment: high_fault_rate co-occurs 1.49x more often than the baseline (segment 37% vs corpus 25%)
Runbook lists backhaul capacity smaller than radio capacity as a likely root cause

hypotheses.cause: A degraded physical transport link, most plausibly affected by weather (for example microwave fading or outdoor fibre or connector problems), which causes packet loss and jitter on the link.
supporting_evidence: Segment: adverse_weather co-occurs 1.58x more often than the baseline (segment 59% vs corpus 37%)
Segment: weather=Rain 1.54x (segment 48% vs corpus 31%) and weather=Snow 1.78x (segment 11% vs corpus 6%)

hypotheses.cause: QoS misconfiguration or a routing change that sends real-time traffic over a longer or congested path, so video calls are not prioritized.
supporting_evidence: The data does not show this link: the segment statistics and similar cases contain no QoS-configuration or routing variables
Runbook lists QoS misconfiguration and routing changes as likely root causes of this symptom pattern

contributing_factors.evidence: adverse_weather co-occurs 1.58x more often than the baseline (segment 59% vs corpus 37%) with high latency and high jitter
weather=Snow co-occurs 1.78x more often than the baseline (segment 11% vs corpus 6%)
high_auth_failures co-occurs 1.55x more often than the baseline (segment 41% vs corpus 26%), but the data does not show whether it is a cause, a symptom or unrelated to transport

data_limitations: KPI values (jitter 44.88 ms, packet loss 11.76 %, latency 116.234 ms, call drop 1.82086 %) are an estimate from similar cases (basis similar_cases_median), not measured values for this incident.
The dataset has no timestamps, cell IDs or topology, so the incident cannot be located or timed, and no trend can be verified.
No radio KPIs (signal strength, handover success) are provided, so separating transport problems from radio problems is not verified by the data.
Severity is relative to this network's history (percentiles), not absolute thresholds.
Correlations in past cases are not proof of causation; lifts describe co-occurrence only.

recommendations.action: Run latency, jitter and packet-loss measurements (TWAMP or ping series) from the affected site to the core and compare against baseline.
recommendations.rationale: Confirms whether latency, jitter and loss are truly degraded on the transport path, as the analysis hypotheses assume.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Establishes the current baseline for latency, jitter and packet loss; no KPI change expected from this check.
recommendations.verification: Measured latency, jitter and loss are recorded against baseline values and the degradation is confirmed or ruled out.

recommendations.action: Check interface counters on the site router and aggregation devices for errors, discards and CRC failures.
recommendations.rationale: Packet loss and jitter may come from a faulty link or interface rather than from congestion alone.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Identifies error or discard sources that would drive packet loss down once fixed.
recommendations.verification: Counters show no growing CRC, error or discard trend over a sampling window of at least one busy-hour period.

recommendations.action: Check backhaul utilization during the affected period and compare it with PRB usage and throughput per user for the cell and its neighbours.
recommendations.rationale: Tests the under-dimensioned backhaul congestion hypothesis shared by TRANSPORT_QOS and CONGESTION_CAPACITY.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Shows whether backhaul near its limit is driving queuing latency, jitter and loss.
recommendations.verification: Utilization trend is compared with latency and loss over the same period; a clear correlation supports congestion as the cause.

recommendations.action: For microwave links, check received signal level and modulation changes; for fibre, check optical power levels, given the adverse weather.
recommendations.rationale: Adverse weather in the contributing factors makes physical link degradation a plausible cause of loss and jitter.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Detects fading or optical degradation that would explain packet loss and jitter.
recommendations.verification: Signal and optical levels are within nominal range, or a degraded level is found and matched to the loss pattern.

recommendations.action: Review recent routing, QoS policy and maintenance changes on the transport path for any change affecting real-time traffic.
recommendations.rationale: A QoS misconfiguration or routing change could send video calls over a longer or congested path, a lower-likelihood hypothesis.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Identifies a misconfigured or changed path that would reduce latency and jitter once corrected.
recommendations.verification: No recent change is found, or any change is documented and its impact on latency and jitter is assessed.

recommendations.action: If backhaul utilization is the cause, increase backhaul capacity or prioritize voice and real-time traffic with QoS marking and queuing, after approval.
recommendations.rationale: Addresses the under-dimensioned transport link that queues real-time video traffic if step 3 confirms congestion.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Latency and jitter decrease and packet loss falls for video calls.
recommendations.verification: Latency, jitter and packet loss return to baseline and stay there for at least one busy-hour period after the change.

escalation.reason: Priority P4 with degradation not yet shown to affect shared aggregation links or several sites; re-evaluate if step 3 or step 4 shows a wider or physical fault.

issues.problem: Step 6 cites KB-TRANSPORT_QOS-corrective-actions and KB-CONGESTION_CAPACITY-diagnostic-checks, which do not appear in the runbook excerpts provided in the evidence digest. Their content is therefore unverified.
issues.fix_instruction: Cite only runbook sections present in the evidence digest (for example KB-TRANSPORT_QOS-diagnostic-checks or KB-TRANSPORT_QOS-likely-root-causes), or remove citations that cannot be traced to the excerpts.

issues.problem: Hypothesis 1 uses the high_fault_rate co-occurrence lift (1.49x) as supporting evidence for backhaul congestion. This is a co-occurrence statistic and does not support a causal link to congestion, which the data limitations themselves state.
issues.fix_instruction: Remove the high_fault_rate lift from the supporting evidence for the congestion hypothesis, or explicitly label it as co-occurrence only that does not establish causation.

issues.problem: The contributing factors table labels adverse weather and snow as 'increases risk', which reads as a causal direction. The evidence only shows co-occurrence lifts, and the data limitations say these are not proof of causation.
issues.fix_instruction: Change the direction wording for weather factors to 'co-occurs with higher risk (association only)' and align the impact narrative with that caveat.

issues.problem: No step checks radio KPIs, even though the runbook KPI signature says radio KPIs are normal for transport problems. The call drop rate anomaly (1.82%, degraded) is also not addressed by any recommendation or verification. Escalation is set to not needed, but the physical-link hypothesis is rated medium with no explicit trigger tied to field-operations escalation criteria.
issues.fix_instruction: Add a step to check radio KPIs (signal strength, handover success) to separate transport from radio causes, add a verification that tracks call drop rate, and state explicit escalation triggers (for example shared aggregation or multi-site degradation, or a confirmed physical fault) that map to the runbook escalation criteria.

validation.summary: The diagnosis is largely grounded in the digest, with correct numbers, citations to present runbook sections, and appropriate change-approval flagging for the disruptive step. It is weakened by a few citations to runbook sections not in the evidence, co-occurrence statistics used as causal support, and gaps in radio-KPI separation, call-drop coverage, and explicit escalation triggers.

### Immediate

Runbook: Congestion and capacity > Diagnostic checks
1. Plot user count, data volume and throughput for the cell and its neighbours over the last 7 days to confirm a load-driven pattern.
2. Compare radio resource utilization (PRB usage) with throughput: high utilization with low throughput per user means radio congestion.
3. Check backhaul link utilization; if it is near its limit, treat the case as transport congestion as well.
4. Check whether neighbouring cells have spare capacity and whether load-balancing features are enabled.
5. Look for abnormal top talkers or device types driving traffic.

Runbook: Congestion and capacity > Corrective actions
### Immediate
- Enable or tune load balancing and traffic steering towards neighbours with headroom (requires change approval).
- Apply temporary QoS prioritization for voice and critical services during the peak.
### Short-term
- Rebalance cell parameters (for example handover offsets or carrier priorities) so edge users move to less loaded cells (requires change approval).
- Activate an additional carrier or bandwidth if licensed spectrum is available (requires change approval).
- Upgrade backhaul capacity if the transport link is the bottleneck.
### Preventive
- Add capacity through cell splitting, small cells or new sectors where growth trends predict sustained congestion.
- Track busy-hour utilization weekly and plan capacity before thresholds are crossed.

answer.summary: Five similar past cases were found, all classified as RADIO_COVERAGE and all rated P3 or P4. The dominant pattern is connection setup success near 90 percent with signal strength around -110 to -120 dBm, and several cases also show configuration-change or transport-quality degradation. The current report has no timestamps, cell IDs or site topology, so the cause cannot be confirmed for this specific site and the recommendations below are a diagnostic sequence rather than a confirmed fix.

likely_causes.cause: Reduced transmit power or antenna settings from a recent configuration error or change, leaving a coverage gap
Coverage hole from antenna tilt or azimuth misalignment, or inadequate site density for the area
Antenna or feeder damage, including water ingress, reducing received signal
Uplink or downlink interference raising the noise floor and degrading call setup
Authentication failures contributing to setup failures (one similar case), possibly independent of radio conditions

recommendations.action: Review recent changes to antenna tilt, azimuth, transmit power and neighbour cells on the affected cells; if a change reduced power or antenna settings, restore planned values (requires change approval).
recommendations.rationale: Recent configuration errors are a direct, fast-to-check cause that matches the immediate corrective action in the runbook.

recommendations.action: Check feeder and antenna alarms and VSWR readings at the serving site, and dispatch field operations if a damaged antenna or feeder is indicated.
recommendations.rationale: Hardware damage would explain the low signal without a configuration change.

recommendations.action: Map the weak-signal and failed-setup reports against predicted coverage of the serving and neighbouring cells, and measure uplink noise rise on the affected cells to separate coverage gaps from interference.
recommendations.rationale: Mapping confirms whether the problem is a geographic hole, and noise measurement tests the interference cause.

recommendations.action: If coverage is confirmed to be a gap, optimize antenna tilt and azimuth to close it (requires change approval), and adjust neighbour relations so edge users are served by the best cell.
recommendations.rationale: Tilt and neighbour tuning are the short-term fixes in the runbook for coverage gaps.

recommendations.action: Plan preventive coverage improvements (new sites, small cells or indoor solutions) for persistent weak areas, and schedule drive tests to detect gaps early if the pattern recurs.
recommendations.rationale: Recurring weak-signal patterns across similar cases suggest structural coverage gaps needing longer-term action.

The current report has no timestamps, cell IDs or site topology, so the cause cannot be confirmed for this specific site and the recommendations below are a diagnostic sequence rather than a confirmed fix.
Likely causes:
- Reduced transmit power or antenna settings from a recent configuration error or change, leaving a coverage gap [KB-RADIO_COVERAGE-likely-root-causes, CASE-076079, CASE-013174]
- Coverage hole from antenna tilt or azimuth misalignment, or inadequate site density for the area [KB-RADIO_COVERAGE-likely-root-causes, CASE-088889, CASE-018327]
- Antenna or feeder damage, including water ingress, reducing received signal [KB-RADIO_COVERAGE-likely-root-causes, KB-RADIO_COVERAGE-diagnostic-checks]
- Uplink or downlink interference raising the noise floor and degrading call setup [KB-RADIO_COVERAGE-likely-root-causes, KB-RADIO_COVERAGE-diagnostic-checks]
- Authentication failures contributing to setup failures (one similar case), possibly independent of radio conditions [CASE-021963]
Recommended actions:
1. Review recent changes to antenna tilt, azimuth, transmit power and neighbour cells on the affected cells; if a change reduced power or antenna settings, restore planned values (requires change approval). Why: Recent configuration errors are a direct, fast-to-check cause that matches the immediate corrective action in the runbook. [KB-RADIO_COVERAGE-diagnostic-checks, KB-RADIO_COVERAGE-corrective-actions, CASE-076079]
2. Check feeder and antenna alarms and VSWR readings at the serving site, and dispatch field operations if a damaged antenna or feeder is indicated. Why: Hardware damage would explain the low signal without a configuration change. [KB-RADIO_COVERAGE-diagnostic-checks, KB-RADIO_COVERAGE-corrective-actions]
3. Map the weak-signal and failed-setup reports against predicted coverage of the serving and neighbouring cells, and measure uplink noise rise on the affected cells to separate coverage gaps from interference. Why: Mapping confirms whether the problem is a geographic hole, and noise measurement tests the interference cause. [KB-RADIO_COVERAGE-diagnostic-checks, CASE-013174]
4. If coverage is confirmed to be a gap, optimize antenna tilt and azimuth to close it (requires change approval), and adjust neighbour relations so edge users are served by the best cell. Why: Tilt and neighbour tuning are the short-term fixes in the runbook for coverage gaps. [KB-RADIO_COVERAGE-corrective-actions, CASE-088889]
5. Plan preventive coverage improvements (new sites, small cells or indoor solutions) for persistent weak areas, and schedule drive tests to detect gaps early if the pattern recurs. Why: Recurring weak-signal patterns across similar cases suggest structural coverage gaps needing longer-term action. [KB-RADIO_COVERAGE-corrective-actions, CASE-018327]

recommendations.action: Check feeder and antenna alarms and VSWR readings at the affected sites.
recommendations.rationale: Antenna or feeder damage or water ingress is the highest-likelihood cause of the coverage hole.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Detects hardware faults that would lower signal strength and call setup success.
recommendations.verification: No active feeder or antenna alarms and VSWR within limits at each site.

recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Shows whether interference is degrading setup success on the uplink.

recommendations.action: Map the weak-signal reports against predicted coverage of the serving and neighbouring cells.

Current KPIs show handover success at 90.91%, call drop at 2.35% and cell availability at 81.9%, but the impact priority is only P4 because it was estimated from median case KPIs rather than live data, so the evidence is indicative rather than conclusive and the causes should be verified against per-neighbour-pair data.

recommendations.action: Check neighbour lists for missing or outdated relations, and check site synchronization alarms at the affected sites.

recommendations.action: Review whether any handover parameter change was made shortly before the failures began; if so, roll back that change (requires change approval).
recommendations.rationale: Rolling back a recent change is the fastest immediate fix when failures started after a change.

recommendations.action: Check target-cell load and admission rejections; relieve overloaded target cells using the congestion runbook if they are rejecting handovers.
recommendations.rationale: Overload is a runbook root cause, and one similar case showed a high user count alongside handover failures.

recommendations.action: Add missing neighbour relations for the worst failing pairs (requires change approval), and fix synchronization issues at the affected sites.
recommendations.rationale: Adds the target-cell preparation needed for handovers and removes timing faults.

recommendations.action: Tune handover offsets, hysteresis and time-to-trigger on the failing pairs against design defaults (requires change approval), then monitor handover success per neighbour pair and alert on sudden drops.
recommendations.rationale: Corrects triggers that act too late or too early and provides early warning of recurrence.

answer.summary: Five similar AVAILABILITY_OUTAGE cases were found (CASE-065782, CASE-089688, CASE-092535, CASE-027494, CASE-067428), all showing the same pattern: cell availability around 77-83% and mean time to repair of roughly 8-10 hours, with fault rates of 15-37%. The cases do not record root causes, so likely causes below come from the runbook and are not confirmed by the data. The evidence pack rates priority P4 from median KPIs, but the runbook says critical availability should be treated as at least P2, so priority should be re-checked against live alarms.

likely_causes.cause: Restoration delays (no spare parts, site access restrictions, or no field staff available) are prolonging outages and driving the long MTTR.
Power failure at the site (mains outage, rectifier or battery failure) causing repeated cell downtime.
Hardware failure of radio or baseband units.
Software crashes or failed upgrades leaving the cell locked or restarting.
Transmission loss, where the site cannot reach the core network.

recommendations.action: Check active alarms for power, hardware and transmission at the site, and confirm whether the cell is down, administratively locked, or restarting repeatedly.
recommendations.rationale: Identifies which root cause applies before choosing a fix; the similar cases do not record causes.

recommendations.action: Check whether neighbouring sites on the same power or transport path are also down, and review recent software upgrades or configuration changes.
recommendations.rationale: Shared power or transport faults and failed upgrades are common causes of repeat cell outages.

recommendations.action: If a failed software upgrade is confirmed, roll it back. If the alarm shows a software or hang condition, attempt a remote restart of the failed unit (requires change approval).
recommendations.rationale: Software faults can be cleared quickly, but remote restarts change the live network and need approval.

recommendations.action: Dispatch field operations for power or hardware failures, treating the cell as at least P2 if availability is critical. Replace failed hardware and restore batteries and rectifiers.
recommendations.rationale: Power and hardware faults need physical repair, and the runbook sets the minimum priority for critical availability.

recommendations.action: Expand neighbour coverage temporarily if parameters allow while the repair is in progress (requires change approval).
recommendations.rationale: Reduces user impact during long repairs, but it changes the network and needs approval.

recommendations.action: Shorten MTTR by checking spare-parts availability, site access and dispatch times, keeping spares at regional depots, and tracking repeat outages per site to fix underlying causes.
recommendations.rationale: Long MTTR across all similar cases points to restoration delays rather than only technical faults.

[KB-AVAILABILITY_OUTAGE-corrective-actions] Cell availability, outage and restoration / corrective-actions
Runbook: Cell availability, outage and restoration > Corrective actions
### Immediate
- Treat critical availability as at least P2; dispatch field operations for power or hardware failures.
- Attempt a remote restart of the failed unit when the alarm indicates a software or hang condition (requires change approval).
- Expand neighbour coverage temporarily if parameters allow (requires change approval).
### Short-term
- Replace failed hardware; restore power systems including batteries and rectifiers.
- Roll back a failed software upgrade.
### Preventive
- Maintain backup power (batteries, generators) sized for expected outage durations.
- Keep spare parts at regional depots to cut MTTR.
- Track repeat outages per site and fix the underlying cause.

[KB-AVAILABILITY_OUTAGE-diagnostic-checks] Cell availability, outage and restoration / diagnostic-checks
Runbook: Cell availability, outage and restoration > Diagnostic checks
1. Check active alarms for power, hardware and transmission at the site.
2. Confirm whether the cell is down, locked administratively, or restarting repeatedly.
3. Check whether neighbouring sites on the same power or transport path are also down.
4. Review recent software upgrades or configuration changes.
5. For long MTTR, check spare-parts availability, site access and field dispatch times.

[KB-AVAILABILITY_OUTAGE-escalation-criteria] Cell availability, outage and restoration / escalation-criteria
Runbook: Cell availability, outage and restoration > Escalation criteria
- Escalate immediately to field operations and the on-call lead for any site down at a busy location.
- Escalate to the vendor or equipment support when hardware or software failures repeat.

[KB-FAULT_ALARM-corrective-actions] Equipment faults and alarm storms / corrective-actions
Runbook: Equipment faults and alarm storms > Corrective actions
### Immediate
- Suppress duplicate secondary alarms and focus on the root alarm.
- Restart the affected software process or unit when the alarm indicates a software hang (requires change approval).
- Dispatch field operations for critical hardware alarms at busy sites.
### Short-term
- Replace faulty hardware; repair cooling systems.
- Apply vendor patches for known software defects (requires change approval).
### Preventive
- Track fault occurrence per site and component; replace units with repeated failures.
- Tune alarm correlation rules so storms are grouped automatically.
- Do proactive maintenance on cooling and power systems before summer.

Likely causes:
1. Failing hardware (radio units, power modules, fans or transceivers) producing repeated faults and a cascade of critical alarms. (likelihood high, evidence: both). Supporting evidence: Fault occurrence rate 49.6812 % (degraded, worse than 79%) per KPI ASSESSMENT; similar-case median estimate; Segment fault-rate co-occurrence 2.86x vs baseline (segment 71% vs corpus 25%); Similar cases CASE-032853 and CASE-080311 show fault rates of 49.7% and 48.6% with high alarm counts; The model fault risk of 0.29 conflicts with the degraded fault rate. The model may not reflect the current KPI state, so this low score is not evidence against the hardware hypothesis [KB-FAULT_ALARM-likely-root-causes, KPI ASSESSMENT, SEGMENT STATS, CASE-032853, CASE-080311, PREDICTIONS]
2. A configuration or parameter change that destabilises equipment and triggers faults and alarms. (likelihood medium, evidence: both). Supporting evidence: Parameter changes 16 changes (degraded, worse than 82%) per KPI ASSESSMENT; similar-case median estimate; CASE-034239 is classified FAULT_ALARM+CONFIG_CHANGE with 16 parameter changes; CASE-080863 is classified FAULT_ALARM+CONFIG_CHANGE with 19 parameter changes (critical) [KPI ASSESSMENT, CASE-034239, CASE-080863]
3. A single upstream transport fault causing an alarm storm, with jitter degrading the links. (likelihood low, evidence: both). Supporting evidence: CASE-034305 is classified FAULT_ALARM+TRANSPORT_QOS with jitter 46.7 ms (critical); KB-FAULT_ALARM-likely-root-causes lists an upstream transport or power fault as a cause of alarm storms; No transport-related lift appears in SEGMENT STATS and the current evidence pack has no direct jitter KPI for this incident [CASE-034305, KB-FAULT_ALARM-likely-root-causes, SEGMENT STATS]
Contributing factors: Snow weather (increases risk): weather=Snow co-occurs 2.36x more often than the baseline (segment 15% vs corpus 6%). Likely causes:
1. Recurring failure of equipment hardware (radio units, power modules, fans or transceivers) producing repeated faults and a burst of critical alarms (likelihood high, evidence: both). Supporting evidence: Fault occurrence rate 49.6812 % (degraded, worse than 79%); high_fault_rate co-occurs 2.86x more often in the segment (71% vs corpus 25%); Median fault occurrence rate in the segment is 51.98%; Runbook lists failing hardware as a likely root cause of alarm storms [KPI ASSESSMENT, SEGMENT STATS, KB-FAULT_ALARM-likely-root-causes]

Supporting evidence: CASE-034305 (FAULT_ALARM+TRANSPORT_QOS, P3) shows jitter 46.7 ms (crit) alongside alarm count 16 alarms (crit) and critical alarm count 10 alarms (crit); Alarm count 16 alarms (critical, worse than 96%); Runbook describes a single upstream transport or power fault as an alarm-storm cause [CASE-034305, KPI ASSESSMENT, KB-FAULT_ALARM-likely-root-causes]

Supporting evidence: Parameter changes 16 changes (degraded, worse than 82%); CASE-034239 and CASE-080863 are FAULT_ALARM+CONFIG_CHANGE cases; Only two of the five similar cases show a configuration-change pattern, and the data has no timestamps to confirm the order of events [KPI ASSESSMENT]

Impact: Impact is Low, with no affected services and 3,154 users served (31st percentile) and 10.44 GB of data. Priority is P4 with a score of 0.291. Recommended actions:
1. Group active alarms by type and site, and identify the first alarm in time to separate the root alarm from secondary alarms. (phase immediate). Why: The storm may start from one root event, which is either recurring hardware failure or a single upstream transport or power fault. Verify: Confirm a single root alarm per site with a clear onset time, and check that the grouped view remains stable for at least one hour. [KB-FAULT_ALARM-diagnostic-checks, CASE-034305]
2. Check hardware health (temperatures, fan status, power-supply readings) at the sites with the most critical alarms. (phase immediate). Why: Hardware faults on radio units, power modules, fans or transceivers are the highest-ranked hypothesis. Verify: Record temperature, fan and power readings per site and confirm they are within normal range or flag the outliers for repair. [KB-FAULT_ALARM-diagnostic-checks]
3. Suppress duplicate secondary alarms so operators focus on the root alarm while the investigation runs. (phase immediate, requires change approval). Why: Duplicate alarms from the storm hide the root cause and inflate the critical alarm count. Verify: Confirm suppressed alarms map to the root alarm and that the true critical fault rate is still tracked for at least 24 hours. [KB-FAULT_ALARM-corrective-actions]
4. Dispatch field operations to sites with critical hardware alarms and recurring faults. (phase immediate). Why: Critical hardware alarms with a high critical fault rate need on-site inspection to confirm or rule out the hardware hypothesis. Verify: Confirm the field report and that critical alarms clear and stay clear for at least 24 hours after the visit. [KB-FAULT_ALARM-corrective-actions, CASE-032853]
5. Check whether the affected sites share a software version, and if a common defect is suspected, prepare a vendor escalation. (phase short_term). Why: A shared software defect across several sites would produce the same alarm burst and triggers vendor escalation. Verify: Confirm the version list per site and check whether the faults cluster on one version over at least one week. [KB-FAULT_ALARM-diagnostic-checks, KB-FAULT_ALARM-escalation-criteria]
6. Replace faulty hardware and repair cooling systems at sites with repeated failures. (phase short_term, requires change approval). Why: Repeated hardware faults at the same sites indicate the component must be replaced, not reset. Verify: Confirm the same alarm type does not recur at the repaired sites for at least two weeks. [KB-FAULT_ALARM-corrective-actions]
7. Track fault occurrence per site and component, and tune alarm correlation rules so future storms are grouped automatically. (phase preventive, requires change approval). Why: Ongoing tracking catches repeat failures early and reduces the manual effort of storm triage. Verify: Review the per-site fault trend monthly and confirm that the next storm is grouped automatically. [KB-FAULT_ALARM-corrective-actions]

recommendations.action: Pull the change log for the affected cells and compare change times with the onset of the configuration success-rate drop.
recommendations.rationale: Matching change timing to degradation onset tests the wrong-parameter-batch hypothesis (high confidence).
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Not a network KPI; establishes which change in the batch is linked to the failures.
recommendations.verification: Change log timestamps are mapped to the failure window and the suspect change set is identified.

recommendations.action: Identify the failed and partially applied changes and record their error messages.
recommendations.rationale: Error messages show whether failures come from invalid values, cell lists or units, or from partial application.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Successful configuration change rate should rise once the failing parameters are corrected.
recommendations.verification: Each failed change has a documented error and a cause, and the list of partially updated cells is complete.

recommendations.action: Compare the current configuration of the affected cells with the last known-good baseline and check whether several teams or tools changed the same cells.
recommendations.rationale: A baseline diff confirms wrong values and detects conflicting or partial changes from other teams or automation (medium confidence).
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Configuration consistency across target cells improves, reducing rollback and fault rates.
recommendations.verification: The diff shows zero unexplained deviations from baseline, or each deviation is documented with its owner.

recommendations.action: Confirm the running software version supports the changed parameters.
recommendations.rationale: Software incompatibility is a lower-likelihood hypothesis that must be ruled out before re-applying changes.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Successful configuration change rate stays stable once compatibility is confirmed.
recommendations.verification: The version compatibility matrix confirms support for every changed parameter.

recommendations.action: Fix the wrong parameter values against the design baseline and re-apply the failed changes or complete the partial ones consistently across all target cells.
recommendations.rationale: Correcting the values and finishing the partial changes addresses the validated root cause.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Successful configuration change rate improves toward its historical level (currently 91.65%).
recommendations.verification: Re-applied changes succeed on all target cells and the success rate holds at or above baseline for at least 24 hours.

recommendations.action: Introduce peer review, test windows and rollback plans for batch parameter changes, and automate configuration-consistency audits against a golden baseline.
recommendations.rationale: Preventive controls reduce the chance of unreviewed parameter sets reaching the network again.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Failed and rolled-back change counts decrease and the success rate stays stable across future batches.
recommendations.verification: The next several batches pass review and audit with no rollbacks, and audit results are tracked per team and tool.

escalation.reason: Impact is low with no affected services and P4 priority; escalate to the change manager only if a change becomes service-affecting, or to the vendor if a software incompatibility is confirmed.

issues.problem: Citations list contains 'SIMILAR CASES' which is not a valid citation key (removed by deterministic check); supporting evidence cites similar-case values that are not labeled with that citation.
issues.fix_instruction: Remove the unknown 'SIMILAR CASES' citation and cite the valid [SIMILAR CASES] evidence only through a recognized key such as KPI ASSESSMENT or SEGMENT STATS, or drop the citation entirely.

issues.problem: The high-likelihood hypothesis is labeled evidence_type 'both' but its runbook-derived part is the KPI signature, and the claim 'wrong parameter set' is a causal inference from co-occurrence of KPI anomalies with no evidence of wrong values.
issues.fix_instruction: Reword the first hypothesis to state that the evidence supports a configuration-change-batch failure pattern, and note explicitly that wrong parameter values are not confirmed by the evidence; keep evidence_type as 'both' only if the runbook is the sole support for the cause.

issues.problem: Contributing factor 'Fault risk model output' cites PREDICTIONS with 'no clear effect' but the fault risk model drivers (weather, alarm_count) are not analysed against the hypotheses; the 'User load' factor cites IMPACT & PRIORITY with a lift from SEGMENT STATS, so citation is mismatched.
issues.fix_instruction: Correct the user-load factor citation to SEGMENT STATS for the lift value, and state that the fault-risk driver values are unavailable so the factor cannot be assessed.

issues.problem: Six recommendations are given, but step 5 (fix values and re-apply changes) is a disruptive change that is placed before verification of root cause, and step 6 (process controls) is not tied to the immediate priority; the immediate rollback/freeze runbook actions are omitted even though the runbook lists them as immediate.
issues.fix_instruction: Add an immediate step to freeze further changes on the affected cells (runbook immediate action) and make step 5 conditional on steps 1-3 confirming the root cause; keep requires_change_approval true for step 5.

issues.problem: Recommendation steps reference 'the affected cells' although the evidence contains no cell IDs or topology, and expected_kpi_effect for step 5 quotes 91.65% which is an estimate from similar cases, not a measured value.
issues.fix_instruction: State that affected cells must first be identified from the change log, and describe the 91.65% figure as an estimated similar-case median rather than a measured baseline.

validation.summary: The diagnosis is broadly consistent with the CONFIG_CHANGE runbook and KPI anomalies, but it contains an invalid citation key and some causal framing beyond the evidence. The recommendations are mostly actionable but omit the runbook's immediate freeze step and rely on unidentified cells.

recommendations.action: Pull the change log for the affected cells and compare change times with the onset of the configuration success-rate drop.
recommendations.rationale: Matching change timing to degradation onset tests the wrong-parameter-batch hypothesis (high confidence).
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Not a network KPI; establishes which change in the batch is linked to the failures.
recommendations.verification: Change log timestamps are mapped to the failure window and the suspect change set is identified.

recommendations.action: Identify the failed and partially applied changes and record their error messages.
recommendations.rationale: Error messages show whether failures come from invalid values, cell lists or units, or from partial application.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Successful configuration change rate should rise once the failing parameters are corrected.
recommendations.verification: Each failed change has a documented error and a cause, and the list of partially updated cells is complete.

recommendations.action: Compare the current configuration of the affected cells with the last known-good baseline and check whether several teams or tools changed the same cells.
recommendations.rationale: A baseline diff confirms wrong values and detects conflicting or partial changes from other teams or automation (medium confidence).
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Configuration consistency across target cells improves, reducing rollback and fault rates.
recommendations.verification: The diff shows zero unexplained deviations from baseline, or each deviation is documented with its owner.

recommendations.action: Confirm the running software version supports the changed parameters.
recommendations.rationale: Software incompatibility is a lower-likelihood hypothesis that must be ruled out before re-applying changes.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Successful configuration change rate stays stable once compatibility is confirmed.
recommendations.verification: The version compatibility matrix confirms support for every changed parameter.

recommendations.action: Fix the wrong parameter values against the design baseline and re-apply the failed changes or complete the partial ones consistently across all target cells.
recommendations.rationale: Correcting the values and finishing the partial changes addresses the validated root cause.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Successful configuration change rate improves toward its historical level (currently 91.65%).
recommendations.verification: Re-applied changes succeed on all target cells and the success rate holds at or above baseline for at least 24 hours.

recommendations.action: Introduce peer review, test windows and rollback plans for batch parameter changes, and automate configuration-consistency audits against a golden baseline.
recommendations.rationale: Preventive controls reduce the chance of unreviewed parameter sets reaching the network again.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Failed and rolled-back change counts decrease and the success rate stays stable across future batches.
recommendations.verification: The next several batches pass review and audit with no rollbacks, and audit results are tracked per team and tool.

escalation.reason: Impact is low with no affected services and P4 priority; escalate to the change manager only if a change becomes service-affecting, or to the vendor if a software incompatibility is confirmed.

answer.summary: Five similar SECURITY_AUTH cases were found, all showing the same dominant pattern: elevated security incidents (around 16-19 per case) alongside degraded authentication failures (18-40 per case), with fault rates between 23% and 48%. The current assessment is P4 (Low) based on median KPIs, since no live KPIs were supplied, and it covers about 3,835 users. Because the evidence contains no timestamps, cell IDs or topology, the cause cannot be pinned down from the data alone, so the recommendations below start with containment and checks that separate a systemic credential or configuration problem from an attack or rogue-device problem.

likely_causes.cause: Signalling or registration flood from compromised or misbehaving devices, consistent with the joint rise in security incidents and authentication failures seen across the similar cases.
Credential problems such as expired certificates or subscriber-data/key mismatches in the authentication chain, which would appear as broad authentication failures.
Misconfiguration of security functions after a recent change, which the runbook lists as a common trigger for this failure pattern.
A rogue base station or spoofing attempt in the area. This is domain knowledge only; none of the similar cases explicitly confirm it.

recommendations.action: Follow the security incident process: isolate and contain before fixing, and preserve core network logs as evidence. Escalate to the security operations team at once if an attack is suspected.
recommendations.rationale: The runbook requires containment before remediation, and the joint security-incident and authentication-failure spike matches the attack pattern.

recommendations.action: Determine whether authentication failures come from many devices (systemic issue) or a small set (abuse or faulty devices), and review failure causes in core logs for unknown subscriber, MAC failure and synchronization failure.
recommendations.rationale: This split decides between a systemic credential or configuration fault and targeted abuse, and the evidence pack does not provide this breakdown.

recommendations.action: Check certificate validity and review recent changes to authentication or security functions, including any clock or time-synchronization issues.
recommendations.rationale: Expired certificates, recent misconfigurations and time-sync errors are the most common root causes listed for this pattern.

recommendations.action: Look for unusual registration rates or signalling patterns, and check for rogue-cell reports or unexpected cell identities in the area.
recommendations.rationale: Registration-rate anomalies point to a flood, and unexpected cell identities point to a rogue base station. Neither is confirmed by the evidence.

recommendations.action: If abusive devices or sources are confirmed, rate-limit or block them. This requires change approval.
recommendations.rationale: The runbook marks blocking as a network change that needs approval, and it should only follow confirmation in step 2.

recommendations.action: Renew expired certificates and correct subscriber-data or key mismatches. If a security configuration change caused the failures, roll it back, which requires change approval.
recommendations.rationale: Short-term remediation depends on what the diagnostics find. Rollback is a network change and needs approval.

recommendations.action: Set alert thresholds on authentication failure rates per cause, automate certificate and key lifecycle management, and schedule a security audit of network functions after recovery.
recommendations.rationale: Preventive measures reduce the chance of recurrence, as recommended in the runbook.

answer.summary: Five similar past cases were found, and all five show the TRANSPORT_QOS pattern, four of them with CONGESTION_CAPACITY. Their median KPIs match this cell's degradation: latency and packet loss are elevated, throughput is reduced, and cell availability is lower. Case CASE-037746 (P2, NV, Summer/Rain) is the most severe, with latency 166.4 ms, packet loss 14.2% and a 90.4% successful-configuration-change rate. The cell is currently assessed as P4 (Low), which is estimated from case medians because no KPIs were supplied. Past cases show correlation only, not proven causation, so the causes below need confirmation with the diagnostic checks.

likely_causes.cause: Backhaul link congestion or an under-dimensioned transport link, which matches the CONGESTION_CAPACITY pattern in the similar cases.
QoS misconfiguration, so real-time traffic is not prioritized, and the recent configuration-change success rate in CASE-037746 suggests configuration instability.
A degraded physical link, such as fibre damage, a dirty connector, or microwave fading or misalignment.
Interface errors or duplex mismatches on routers and switches.
Routing changes that send traffic over a longer or congested path, which may also reduce availability as seen in CASE-005057.

recommendations.action: Run latency, jitter and loss measurements (for example TWAMP or ping series) from the site to the core and compare them with the baseline, and review recent transport changes for routing, QoS policies and maintenance.
recommendations.rationale: Confirms whether the degradation is ongoing and checks the change history for a trigger.

recommendations.action: Check interface counters on the site router and aggregation devices for errors, discards and CRC failures, and check backhaul utilization for the affected period.
recommendations.rationale: Separates congestion from interface faults or duplex issues.

recommendations.action: Check the physical layer: for microwave links, check received signal level and modulation changes; for fibre, check optical power levels.
recommendations.rationale: Identifies a degraded physical link if counters or utilization do not explain the loss.

recommendations.action: Prioritize voice and real-time traffic with QoS marking and queuing if the policy is missing or wrong (requires change approval). Reroute traffic to a backup or protection path if one is available (requires change approval).
recommendations.rationale: Immediate mitigation for loss and latency while the root cause is fixed.

recommendations.action: Repair or replace degraded physical components, correct duplex or MTU mismatches, and increase backhaul capacity if utilization is the cause.
recommendations.rationale: Addresses the confirmed root cause from the diagnostics.

recommendations.action: Set alerts on latency, jitter and loss trends, and plan path diversity for this site if it is critical.
recommendations.rationale: Preventive measure to catch recurrence early.

A.actual_output:
Summary: Five similar past cases were found, and all five show the TRANSPORT_QOS pattern, four of them with CONGESTION_CAPACITY. Their median KPIs match this cell's degradation: latency and packet loss are elevated, throughput is reduced, and cell availability is lower. Case CASE-037746 (P2, NV, Summer/Rain) is the most severe, with latency 166.4 ms, packet loss 14.2% and a 90.4% successful-configuration-change rate. The cell is currently assessed as P4 (Low), which is estimated from case medians because no KPIs were supplied. Past cases show correlation only, not proven causation, so the causes below need confirmation with the diagnostic checks.
Likely causes:
- Backhaul link congestion or an under-dimensioned transport link, which matches the CONGESTION_CAPACITY pattern in the similar cases. [KB-TRANSPORT_QOS-likely-root-causes, CASE-037746, CASE-016229, CASE-039539, CASE-050747]
- QoS misconfiguration, so real-time traffic is not prioritized, and the recent configuration-change success rate in CASE-037746 suggests configuration instability. [KB-TRANSPORT_QOS-likely-root-causes, CASE-037746]
- A degraded physical link, such as fibre damage, a dirty connector, or microwave fading or misalignment. [KB-TRANSPORT_QOS-likely-root-causes]
- Interface errors or duplex mismatches on routers and switches. [KB-TRANSPORT_QOS-likely-root-causes]
- Routing changes that send traffic over a longer or congested path, which may also reduce availability as seen in CASE-005057. [KB-TRANSPORT_QOS-likely-root-causes, CASE-005057]
Recommended actions:
1. Run latency, jitter and loss measurements (for example TWAMP or ping series) from the site to the core and compare them with the baseline, and review recent transport changes for routing, QoS policies and maintenance. Why: Confirms whether the degradation is ongoing and checks the change history for a trigger. [KB-TRANSPORT_QOS-diagnostic-checks, CASE-037746]
2. Check interface counters on the site router and aggregation devices for errors, discards and CRC failures, and check backhaul utilization for the affected period. Why: Separates congestion from interface faults or duplex issues. [KB-TRANSPORT_QOS-diagnostic-checks, KB-TRANSPORT_QOS-likely-root-causes, CASE-016229]
3. Check the physical layer: for microwave links, check received signal level and modulation changes; for fibre, check optical power levels. Why: Identifies a degraded physical link if counters or utilization do not explain the loss. [KB-TRANSPORT_QOS-diagnostic-checks]
4. Prioritize voice and real-time traffic with QoS marking and queuing if the policy is missing or wrong (requires change approval). Reroute traffic to a backup or protection path if one is available (requires change approval). Why: Immediate mitigation for loss and latency while the root cause is fixed. [KB-TRANSPORT_QOS-corrective-actions, CASE-037746]
5. Repair or replace degraded physical components, correct duplex or MTU mismatches, and increase backhaul capacity if utilization is the cause. Why: Addresses the confirmed root cause from the diagnostics. [KB-TRANSPORT_QOS-corrective-actions, CASE-039539]
6. Set alerts on latency, jitter and loss trends, and plan path diversity for this site if it is critical. Why: Preventive measure to catch recurrence early. [KB-TRANSPORT_QOS-corrective-actions]

[KB-TRANSPORT_QOS-likely-root-causes] Transport and QoS degradation (latency, jitter, packet loss) / likely-root-causes
Runbook: Transport and QoS degradation (latency, jitter, packet loss) > Likely root causes
- Backhaul link congestion or an under-dimensioned transport link.
- A degraded physical link: fibre damage, a dirty connector, microwave fading or misalignment.
- Interface errors or duplex mismatches on routers and switches.
- QoS misconfiguration, so real-time traffic is not prioritized.
- Routing changes that send traffic over a longer or congested path.

[KB-TRANSPORT_QOS-diagnostic-checks] Transport and QoS degradation (latency, jitter, packet loss) / diagnostic-checks
Runbook: Transport and QoS degradation (latency, jitter, packet loss) > Diagnostic checks
1. Run latency, jitter and loss measurements (for example TWAMP or ping series) from the site to the core and compare with the baseline.
2. Check interface counters on the site router and aggregation devices for errors, discards and CRC failures.
3. Check backhaul utilization during the affected period.
4. For microwave links, check received signal level and modulation changes; for fibre, check optical power levels.
5. Review recent transport changes: routing, QoS policies, maintenance.

[KB-TRANSPORT_QOS-corrective-actions] Transport and QoS degradation (latency, jitter, packet loss) / corrective-actions
Runbook: Transport and QoS degradation (latency, jitter, packet loss) > Corrective actions
### Immediate
- Reroute traffic to a backup or protection path if available (requires change approval).
- Prioritize voice and real-time traffic with QoS marking and queuing if the policy is missing or wrong (requires change approval).
### Short-term
- Repair or replace degraded physical components: clean or replace connectors, realign microwave antennas, repair fibre.
- Correct interface configuration issues such as duplex or MTU mismatches.
- Increase backhaul capacity where utilization is the cause.
### Preventive
- Monitor transport KPIs continuously with alerts on latency, jitter and loss trends.
- Build path diversity for critical sites.

recommendations.action: Run latency, jitter and packet loss measurements from the site to the core and compare them with the baseline.
recommendations.rationale: Confirms whether the transport path is the source of the latency and loss, which is the primary hypothesis.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: No change expected; establishes the baseline needed to judge later improvement.
recommendations.verification: Measurement series shows latency, jitter and loss values documented against the baseline for the affected period.

recommendations.action: Check interface counters on the site router and aggregation devices for errors, discards and CRC failures.
recommendations.rationale: Physical or interface faults are a likely cause of packet loss on the transport link.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Packet loss rate should fall once any error source is found and fixed.
recommendations.verification: Counters are reviewed for the affected window and any growth in errors or discards is identified.

recommendations.action: Check backhaul utilization during the affected period and review recent routing, QoS and maintenance changes.
recommendations.rationale: Tests the high-likelihood backhaul congestion hypothesis and looks for a recent change that may have caused it.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Confirms or rules out backhaul saturation as the cause of latency and throughput loss.
recommendations.verification: Utilization trend and change log are reviewed; saturation near link limits is either confirmed or excluded.

recommendations.action: For microwave links, check received signal level and modulation; for fibre, check optical power levels.
recommendations.rationale: Adverse weather and physical link degradation are a medium-likelihood hypothesis supported by similar rain and winter cases.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: If signal or optical power is degraded, correcting it should reduce packet loss and improve throughput.
recommendations.verification: Signal or optical levels are within expected range and packet loss stays low for at least 24 hours after any repair.

recommendations.action: Plot user count, data volume and PRB utilization against throughput for the cell and its neighbours over the last 7 days.
recommendations.rationale: Tests the lower-likelihood radio-side congestion hypothesis and rules it in or out.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Confirms whether throughput loss follows a load pattern; no direct KPI change.
recommendations.verification: Load and throughput plots show whether high PRB use coincides with low per-user throughput.

recommendations.action: If the policy is missing or wrong, prioritize voice and real-time traffic with QoS marking and queuing.
recommendations.rationale: Poor real-time prioritization is a high-likelihood cause of latency and loss, so QoS correction is a candidate fix once diagnostics confirm it.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Latency and packet loss for real-time traffic should decrease; throughput should stabilise.
recommendations.verification: Latency and packet loss recover to baseline and remain stable for at least 24 hours after the change.

recommendations.action: Set alerts on transport latency, jitter and loss trends for the site.
recommendations.rationale: Early alerting would catch recurrence of the transport degradation seen in similar cases.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Earlier detection of latency and loss trends, reducing time to respond.
recommendations.verification: Alerts fire in a test condition and are confirmed in the monitoring system.

escalation.reason: Priority P4 with no evidence yet of shared aggregation links or multi-site impact; escalate to the transport or IP team if shared links are affected, or to field operations if physical repair is required.

issues.problem: Steps 6 and 7 cite KB-TRANSPORT_QOS-corrective-actions, which is not among the runbook excerpts provided. The deterministic citations_valid PASS is therefore inconsistent with the evidence.
issues.fix_instruction: Cite only runbook sections present in the evidence digest (for example KB-TRANSPORT_QOS-diagnostic-checks or KB-TRANSPORT_QOS-escalation-criteria). If no supporting section exists for QoS changes or alerting, remove the citation or state that the step is not runbook-backed.

issues.problem: The analyst infers that high_critical_alarms 'points towards equipment faults rather than load'. The segment stats are co-occurrence lifts only, so this is a causal-style claim the evidence does not support.
issues.fix_instruction: Describe the alarm and fault-rate lifts strictly as co-occurrence with the segment. Do not use them to rule causes in or out, and label any equipment-fault reading as a hypothesis needing verification.

issues.problem: Hypothesis 1 is titled as transport or backhaul congestion, but its first supporting point relies on CONGESTION_CAPACITY labels from similar cases. This blurs the transport and congestion categories that the analysis is meant to separate.
issues.fix_instruction: Base hypothesis 1 on TRANSPORT_QOS evidence and the transport KPI signature. Mention CONGESTION_CAPACITY co-labels separately as a point that needs to be distinguished from transport causes.

issues.problem: Step 3 bundles three distinct checks (backhaul utilization, routing changes, QoS and maintenance changes) into one action, which makes its verification and pass or fail outcome harder to assess.
issues.fix_instruction: Split step 3 into separate actions: one for backhaul utilization and one for reviewing recent routing, QoS and maintenance changes, each with its own verification.

validation.summary: The diagnosis is mostly grounded and its hypotheses match the TRANSPORT_QOS KPI pattern, with sensible ordering and change approval flagged for the QoS step. However, two recommendations cite a runbook section absent from the evidence, and the analyst overreaches by treating co-occurrence lifts as evidence for equipment faults.

recommendations.action: Run latency, jitter and packet loss measurements from the site to the core and compare them with the baseline.

recommendations.action: Check interface counters on the site router and aggregation devices for errors, discards and CRC failures.
recommendations.rationale: Physical or interface faults are a likely cause of packet loss on the transport link.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Packet loss rate should fall once any error source is found and fixed.
recommendations.verification: Counters are reviewed for the affected window and any growth in errors or discards is identified.

recommendations.action: Check backhaul utilization during the affected period and review recent routing, QoS and maintenance changes.
recommendations.rationale: Tests the high-likelihood backhaul congestion hypothesis and looks for a recent change that may have caused it.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Confirms or rules out backhaul saturation as the cause of latency and throughput loss.
recommendations.verification: Utilization trend and change log are reviewed; saturation near link limits is either confirmed or excluded.

recommendations.action: For microwave links, check received signal level and modulation; for fibre, check optical power levels.
recommendations.rationale: Adverse weather and physical link degradation are a medium-likelihood hypothesis supported by similar rain and winter cases.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: If signal or optical power is degraded, correcting it should reduce packet loss and improve throughput.
recommendations.verification: Signal or optical levels are within expected range and packet loss stays low for at least 24 hours after any repair.

recommendations.action: Plot user count, data volume and PRB utilization against throughput for the cell and its neighbours over the last 7 days.
recommendations.rationale: Tests the lower-likelihood radio-side congestion hypothesis and rules it in or out.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Confirms whether throughput loss follows a load pattern; no direct KPI change.
recommendations.verification: Load and throughput plots show whether high PRB use coincides with low per-user throughput.

recommendations.action: If the policy is missing or wrong, prioritize voice and real-time traffic with QoS marking and queuing.
recommendations.rationale: Poor real-time prioritization is a high-likelihood cause of latency and loss, so QoS correction is a candidate fix once diagnostics confirm it.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Latency and packet loss for real-time traffic should decrease; throughput should stabilise.
recommendations.verification: Latency and packet loss recover to baseline and remain stable for at least 24 hours after the change.

recommendations.rationale: Early alerting would catch recurrence of the transport degradation seen in similar cases.
recommendations.expected_kpi_effect: Earlier detection of latency and loss trends, reducing time to respond.

answer.summary: Five similar past cases were found, all classified as FAULT_ALARM, and they share a dominant pattern of critical alarm counts (about 15) with cell availability near 80% and signal strength around -107 dBm. Several cases also show availability outage or radio coverage problems, which fits an alarm storm driven by one or more underlying equipment or upstream faults. The data has no timestamps, cell IDs or topology, so the root cause cannot be confirmed; the correlations in these cases do not prove causation. The impact estimate is P4 (Low), derived from median case KPIs because no live KPIs were supplied, so it should be checked against live data.

likely_causes.cause: Failing hardware (radio units, power modules, fans, transceivers) producing repeated critical alarms and signal degradation across affected cells.
A single upstream fault (transport or power) raising many secondary alarms at once, creating an alarm storm that degrades availability across several cells.
Over-temperature from cooling failure, which can trigger hardware alarms and availability loss, with higher risk in hot periods.
Software defects or memory leaks causing repeated restarts or hangs on affected units, possibly as a common-mode defect shared by a software version.
Previous repairs that treated symptoms only, so the fault is recurring; similar cases show high fault rates (about 29% to 47%).

recommendations.action: Group active alarms by type and site, separate the root alarm from secondary alarms, and suppress duplicate secondary alarms so the root event is visible. Identify the first alarm in time to locate the storm's origin.
recommendations.rationale: Storms usually start from one root event, and the runbook's first immediate action is to focus on the root alarm.

recommendations.action: Check hardware health at the affected sites: temperatures, fan status and power-supply readings. Check each site's fault history for recurring alarm types and whether affected sites share a software version.
recommendations.rationale: These checks distinguish hardware, cooling, power and common-mode software causes, which the case data cannot separate on its own.

recommendations.action: Investigate any upstream transport or power fault that could explain simultaneous alarms across several cells, and check for packet loss on the transport path.

C.actual_output:
Likely causes:
1. A hardware or equipment fault (for example radio units, power or transceivers) producing an alarm storm that raises fault occurrence and degrades handovers. This hypothesis is unconfirmed: the support is co-occurrence in similar cases, and no neighbour or parameter data is available to test it. (likelihood medium, evidence: both). Supporting evidence: Similar-case median estimate: fault occurrence rate 48.3305 % (degraded, worse than 75% of records); Similar-case median estimate: handover success rate 91 % (critical, worse than 90% of records); high_critical_alarms co-occurs 2.86x more often than the corpus baseline (segment 72% vs corpus 25%); Segment of 6263 matching historical cases; co-occurrence only, not causation [KPI ASSESSMENT, SEGMENT STATS, CASE-095819, KB-FAULT_ALARM-likely-root-causes]
2. Mobility misconfiguration, such as missing or wrong neighbour relations or handover thresholds, timers or offsets that trigger handovers too late or too early. The data does not show this link: no neighbour or parameter data is available, and the parameter-change evidence is limited to one similar case. (likelihood low, evidence: knowledge). Supporting evidence: Runbook lists missing neighbour relations and mis-set handover thresholds as likely causes of low handover success; CASE-052688 (ME/Summer/Clear) shows handover success 90.1% (crit) with parameter changes 16 changes (deg); No neighbour relation or parameter data is present in the evidence pack, so this cause cannot be tested [KB-MOBILITY_HANDOVER-likely-root-causes, CASE-052688]
3. Target-cell overload, where user load causes incoming handovers to be rejected. The region serves a relatively high user count, but the evidence does not show load-related handover failures directly. (likelihood low, evidence: data). Supporting evidence: user_count is among the top drivers of the fault risk model; 6,933 users served (more than 69% of records); No cell-level load or handover rejection data is available [PREDICTIONS, KB-MOBILITY_HANDOVER-likely-root-causes]
Contributing factors: Snow / winter weather (increases risk): weather=Snow co-occurs 3.03x more often than the corpus baseline (segment 19% vs corpus 6%); adverse_weather co-occurs 2.16x (segment 81% vs corpus 37%). Co-occurrence only; the data does not establish that weather causes the incident.; Security and authentication failures (increases risk): high_auth_failures co-occurs 2.63x more often than baseline (segment 69% vs corpus 26%). CASE-095819 (MN/Winter/Snow) shows authentication failures 35 failures (crit) alongside handover success 90.5% (crit).; Summer / clear conditions (no clear effect): CASE-052688 (ME/Summer/Clear) shows a similar handover and fault pattern (handover success 90.1% crit, fault rate 49.4%), so the pattern is not limited to winter cases.
Impact: The incident affects voice services for about 6,933 users, a population at the 69th percentile of this network's records, and 17.24 GB of data. Impact is rated High and priority P3 (Medium). The KPI values underlying this assessment are estimates from the median of similar cases, not measured values for this region.
Data limitations: The query describes increasing fault occurrence and declining handover success, but the dataset has no timestamps or time series, so trends cannot be verified. No season comparison for this region is available; only similar cases by season are shown.; KPI values are estimates from the similar-case median (basis: similar_cases_median), not measured values for this region.; No neighbour relation, parameter, topology or cell-level data is available, so mobility misconfiguration and cell overload cannot be tested.; Segment lifts and similar-case patterns are co-occurrence, not causation.; The query asks for corrective actions; this analysis does not recommend actions.; The performance model reports a 27.1% deficit while observed throughput (495.255 Mbps) is above expected (389.7 Mbps); the sign is inconsistent and should be treated with caution.; Severity hint is unknown and the classification confidence is 0.6 (llm), so the primary and secondary classes are not fully certain.; The dataset is synthetic and severity is relative to this network's percentiles, not absolute thresholds.
Recommended actions:
1. Break down handover failures by target cell and produce a ranked list of failing neighbour pairs with their handover success values. (phase immediate). Why: The runbook's first diagnostic check identifies which neighbour pairs drive the handover success decline, which tests the mobility hypothesis. Verify: A ranked list of failing neighbour pairs with their handover success values is produced and reviewed. [KB-MOBILITY_HANDOVER-diagnostic-checks]
2. Suppress duplicate secondary alarms and focus the operator view on the root alarm at the affected equipment. (phase immediate). Why: The high fault rate fits the alarm-storm hypothesis, so grouping secondary alarms exposes the root hardware fault. Verify: Fault occurrence rate per site is tracked for 24 hours and shows a sustained decline after root alarms are isolated. [KB-FAULT_ALARM-corrective-actions]
3. Dispatch field operations for any critical hardware alarms at busy sites, such as radio units, power or transceivers. (phase immediate). Why: Critical hardware alarms at busy sites are the most likely source of the alarm storm and the handover degradation. Verify: Fault occurrence rate at the dispatched sites is compared before and after the visit over the following 24 hours. [KB-FAULT_ALARM-corrective-actions]
4. Add missing neighbour relations for the worst failing pairs identified in step 1, if the neighbour list check confirms them. (phase short_term, requires change approval). Why: Missing or outdated neighbour relations on the failing pairs would cause handover failures that the diagnostic checks can confirm. Verify: Handover success on the corrected pairs is compared with the ranked list from step 1 and holds for 24 hours. [KB-MOBILITY_HANDOVER-corrective-actions, KB-MOBILITY_HANDOVER-diagnostic-checks]
5. Check target-cell load, admission rejections and site synchronization alarms for the failing pairs. (phase short_term). Why: This tests the target-cell overload and synchronization hypotheses, which the data does not yet confirm. Verify: Load and admission rejection values and any synchronization alarms are documented per failing pair. [KB-MOBILITY_HANDOVER-diagnostic-checks]
6. Replace faulty hardware and repair cooling systems at the sites confirmed by the alarm analysis. (phase short_term, requires change approval). Why: Confirmed hardware faults are the likely driver of the alarm storm and the fault occurrence increase. Verify: Fault occurrence rate at the repaired sites is confirmed to stay below its pre-repair level for 48 hours. [KB-FAULT_ALARM-corrective-actions]
7. Track fault occurrence per site and component, and replace units with repeated failures. (phase preventive). Why: Repeated failures at the same units indicate a recurring hardware problem that needs proactive replacement. Verify: A per-site, per-component fault count is reviewed weekly and shows no repeat failures on replaced units. [KB-FAULT_ALARM-corrective-actions]
Escalation: needed, RAN optimization. Neighbour or parameter changes on the failing pairs require RAN optimization review if the diagnostic checks confirm them.
